groups.name: Islamic
groups.note: Reference point for most seed leads; compared with every tradition.

leads.title: Abraham smashes the idols
leads.summary: In Genesis Rabbah, Abraham smashes the idols in his father's shop, blames the largest one, and is thrown into a furnace by Nimrod. In the Quran, Abraham breaks the idols except the biggest, tells the people to ask them, and is thrown into a fire made cool.

leads.title: Instruction of Amenemope and Proverbs 22–24
leads.summary: Proverbs 22:17–24:22 closely parallels the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, including the 'thirty sayings' framing.

leads.title: The Buddha becomes a Christian saint
leads.summary: The life of the Buddha passed through Manichaean and Arabic versions (Bilawhar wa-Būdhāsf) into the Georgian Balavariani and the Greek Barlaam and Ioasaph. Josaphat became a saint in the Christian calendar.
evidence: The name chain bodhisattva → Būdhāsaf → Yūdāsaf → Iōasaph is the lexical spine of the lead.

leads.title: The raven that teaches burial
leads.summary: In the Quran a raven shows Cain how to bury Abel. In Pirqei de-Rabbi Eliezer a raven shows Adam and Eve.
evidence: Who learns from the raven differs (Cain vs. Adam). Dating PRE relative to the Quran is part of the question.

leads.title: Jesus brings clay birds to life
leads.summary: In the Infancy Gospel of Thomas the child Jesus shapes sparrows from clay and makes them fly. The Quran has Jesus fashion birds from clay that become birds by God's permission.
evidence: The Quran adds 'by God's permission' (bi-idhnī), which reframes the miracle theologically. That is a response-type detail.

leads.title: Dhul-Qarnayn and the Alexander legends
leads.summary: The Quran's Dhul-Qarnayn travels to where the sun sets and rises and builds a barrier against Gog and Magog. The Syriac Alexander Legend and the Alexander Romance have close parallels.
evidence: The Syriac Legend is often dated around 630 (Reinink), close to the Quran. The direction and the dating are both debated.

leads.title: Flood narratives across traditions
leads.summary: A divinely sent flood with a chosen survivor appears in Sumerian, Akkadian, Hebrew, Quranic, Vedic, Greek, and Chinese sources. The Near Eastern versions are historically linked; the others are candidate convergences.

passages.ref: Shujing; Mencius (Gun and Yu tame the flood)

evidence: Specificity test: the bird-release sequence (Gilgamesh XI; Genesis 8) is a rare motif combination that marks the Mesopotamian–Hebrew link. The Quran has no bird release.
Noah's drowned son (Quran 11:42–43) has no Genesis counterpart and is a sub-lead.
The Chinese story is about controlling the flood, not surviving it, so it is a weak match.

leads.title: Han Kitab: Islam in Neo-Confucian terms
leads.summary: Chinese Muslim scholars such as Wang Daiyu and Liu Zhi expressed tawḥīd with Neo-Confucian metaphysics: 真一 'the Real One', li and qi, and the Supreme Ultimate, in dialogue with Zhu Xi.

passages.ref: Zhu Xi, commentaries; Zhou Dunyi, Taijitu shuo

leads.title: haykal: the Sumerian 'big house'
leads.summary: Sumerian é-gal ('big house', palace) became Akkadian ekallu, Hebrew hêkhāl (palace, temple), Aramaic hêkhlā, and Arabic haykal.
evidence: haykal does not occur in the Quran; it is a control case for the lexical track.

leads.title: Satan refuses to bow to Adam
leads.summary: God commands the angels to honor Adam, and Satan refuses. Found in the Life of Adam and Eve and the Cave of Treasures, and repeatedly in the Quran.

passages.ref: Life of Adam and Eve (Latin Vita 12–16)

evidence: Iblis's argument from substance, fire vs. clay (7:12, 38:76): check whether the Syriac sources make the same argument.

leads.title: The Kalam cosmological argument
leads.summary: The argument that the universe began and so has a cause, developed by the mutakallimūn and al-Ghazali, was revived and named by William Lane Craig in analytic philosophy of religion.

passages.ref: W. L. Craig, The Kalām Cosmological Argument (1979)

leads.title: Panchatantra to Kalila wa-Dimna
leads.summary: The Sanskrit Panchatantra was translated into Middle Persian (Burzoy, 6th c.), then Arabic (Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ, 8th c.), then into Hebrew, Greek, Latin, and most European languages.

leads.title: Kumarbi cycle and Hesiod's Theogony
leads.summary: Both have the same succession myth: Anu, Kumarbi, Teshub in the Hurro-Hittite cycle and Ouranos, Kronos, Zeus in Hesiod, including a sky god castrated by his successor.

leads.title: kursī: Sumerian throne to Quranic seat
leads.summary: Sumerian guza passed into Akkadian kussû, Aramaic kursēʾ, and Arabic kursī. The Quran's Throne Verse (2:255) uses it.

passages.note: His kursī encompasses the heavens and the earth

evidence: Arabic kursī shows the Aramaic -r- form (dissimilated -ss- > -rs-), which points to Aramaic as the immediate source.

leads.title: Mani and the 'seal of the prophets'
leads.summary: Quran 33:40 calls Muhammad khātam al-nabiyyīn. Manichaean sources present Mani as the last in a line of prophets (Buddha, Zoroaster, Jesus), and whether 'seal' was a Manichaean title is debated.

passages.ref: Kephalaia 1; al-Biruni's quotation of the Shābuhragān

evidence: See Stroumsa, 'Seal of the Prophets: The Nature of a Manichaean Metaphor' (1986), for the case against reading it as a Manichaean title.

leads.title: Mary raised in the Temple
leads.summary: The Protevangelium of James has Mary dedicated to the Temple, fed by an angel, and her guardian chosen by a sign. The Quran has Mary's dedication, miraculous provision in the sanctuary, Zechariah as guardian, and lots cast for her care.

leads.title: Mary and the palm tree
leads.summary: In Pseudo-Matthew a palm bends to feed Mary and a spring opens during the flight to Egypt. In the Quran a palm and a stream sustain Mary during the birth of Jesus.
evidence: The setting moves from the flight to Egypt to the birth itself.

leads.title: rāgha: a turned word concentrated in Abraham
leads.summary: راغَ (rāgha, “turned”) occurs in 3 verses; 3 of them (100%) are in the Abraham narrative, which is 3% of the Quran, across 2 surahs. The more common same-gloss word قَلَّبُ (qallabu, 6 verses) has only 0% of its verses there.
evidence: p = 2.2e-05 (hypergeometric, verse level), q = 1.1e-04.

leads.title: yahbiṭu: a down word concentrated in Adam and Iblis
leads.summary: يَهْبِطُ (yahbiṭu, “down”) occurs in 8 verses; 5 of them (62%) are in the Adam and Iblis narrative, which is 1% of the Quran, across 3 surahs. The more common same-gloss word نَزَّلَ (nazzala, 61 verses) has only 0% of its verses there.
evidence: p = 1.0e-08 (hypergeometric, verse level), q = 1.8e-07.

leads.title: ʾaṣnām: a word shared by Abraham and Moses
leads.summary: أَصْنام (ʾaṣnām, “idol”) occurs in 5 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Abraham (4) and Moses (1). A rare word linking two stories.
evidence: p = 9.0e-06 (hypergeometric, verse level).

leads.title: baqara: a word shared by Joseph and Moses
leads.summary: بَقَرَة (baqara, “cow”) occurs in 6 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Joseph (2) and Moses (4). A rare word linking two stories.

lexical.gloss: beef cattle or an animal of the ox family of either gender (as used for plowing) (H1241, possible cognate)

evidence: p = 3.9e-07 (hypergeometric, verse level).
Hebrew cognates are matched by regular sound correspondence plus a shared gloss word in Strong's definition; check them before relying on them.

leads.title: ḍayf: a word shared by Abraham and Lot
leads.summary: ضَيْف (ḍayf, “guest”) occurs in 5 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Abraham (2) and Lot (3). A rare word linking two stories.
evidence: p = 8.1e-08 (hypergeometric, verse level).

leads.title: fitya: a word shared by People of the Cave and Joseph
leads.summary: فِتْيَة (fitya, “youth”) occurs in 3 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: People of the Cave (2) and Joseph (1). A rare word linking two stories.
evidence: p = 6.3e-06 (hypergeometric, verse level).

leads.title: ḥūt: a word shared by Jonah and Moses
leads.summary: حُوت (ḥūt, “fish”) occurs in 5 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Jonah (2) and Moses (3). A rare word linking two stories.
evidence: p = 2.0e-06 (hypergeometric, verse level).

leads.title: rahṭ: a word shared by Salih and Thamud and Shuʿayb and Midian
leads.summary: رَهْط (rahṭ, “family”) occurs in 3 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Salih and Thamud (1) and Shuʿayb and Midian (2). A rare word linking two stories.
evidence: p = 2.4e-06 (hypergeometric, verse level).

leads.title: rāwadu: a word shared by Joseph and Lot
leads.summary: راوَدُ (rāwadu, “seduce”) occurs in 7 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Joseph (6) and Lot (1). A rare word linking two stories.
evidence: p = 7.3e-12 (hypergeometric, verse level).

leads.title: tābūt: a word shared by Moses and Saul (Talut) and Goliath
leads.summary: تابُوت (tābūt, “ark”) occurs in 2 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Moses (1) and Saul (Talut) and Goliath (1). A rare word linking two stories.
evidence: p = 5.1e-03 (hypergeometric, verse level).
The Quranic Arabic Corpus gives no root, which often marks a loanword.
Hebrew cognate תֵּבָה (H8392) is itself a rare word linking two Hebrew Bible narratives: Moses (2) and Noah and the Flood (23). Both words connect stories, and they share at least one.
Hebrew cognates are matched by regular sound correspondence plus a shared gloss word in Strong's definition; check them before relying on them.

leads.title: ṭafiqa: a word shared by Adam and Iblis and Solomon
leads.summary: طَفِقَ (ṭafiqa, “began”) occurs in 3 verses, all or nearly all inside two narratives: Adam and Iblis (2) and Solomon (1). A rare word linking two stories.
evidence: p = 6.8e-06 (hypergeometric, verse level).

leads.title: ghābir: a behind word concentrated in Lot
leads.summary: غابِر (ghābir, “behind”) occurs in 7 verses; 5 of them (71%) are in the Lot narrative, which is 1% of the Quran, across 4 surahs. The more common same-gloss word خَلْف (khalf, 22 verses) has only 0% of its verses there.
evidence: p = 2.2e-09 (hypergeometric, verse level), q = 4.5e-08.

leads.title: akhtāra: a chose word concentrated in Moses
leads.summary: اخْتارَ (akhtāra, “chose”) occurs in 4 verses; 3 of them (75%) are in the Moses narrative, which is 7% of the Quran, across 3 surahs. The more common same-gloss word اجْتَبَى (ajtabā, 10 verses) has only 0% of its verses there.
evidence: p = 1.3e-03 (hypergeometric, verse level), q = 3.4e-03.

leads.title: ʾānasa: a perceive word concentrated in Moses
leads.summary: آنَسَ (ʾānasa, “perceive”) occurs in 4 verses; 3 of them (75%) are in the Moses narrative, which is 7% of the Quran, across 3 surahs. The more common same-gloss word يَشْعُرُ (yashʿuru, 25 verses) has only 8% of its verses there.
evidence: p = 1.3e-03 (hypergeometric, verse level), q = 3.4e-03.

leads.title: ʾayman: a right word concentrated in Moses
leads.summary: أَيْمَن (ʾayman, “right”) occurs in 3 verses; 3 of them (100%) are in the Moses narrative, which is 7% of the Quran, across 3 surahs. The more common same-gloss word قَيِّم (qayyim, 5 verses) has only 0% of its verses there.

lexical.gloss: right (i.e. at the right hand) (H3233, possible cognate)
to be right-handed or take the right-hand side (H3231, possible cognate)

evidence: p = 3.4e-04 (hypergeometric, verse level), q = 1.1e-03.
Hebrew cognates are matched by regular sound correspondence plus a shared gloss word in Strong's definition; check them before relying on them.

leads.title: salwā: a quail word concentrated in Moses
leads.summary: سَلْوَى (salwā, “quail”) occurs in 3 verses; 3 of them (100%) are in the Moses narrative, which is 7% of the Quran, across 3 surahs.

lexical.gloss: the quail collectively (as slow in flight from its weight) (H7958, possible cognate)

evidence: p = 3.4e-04 (hypergeometric, verse level), q = 1.1e-03.
Hebrew cognate שְׂלָו (H7958) is also concentrated in the same narrative in the Hebrew Bible (75% of its verses).
Hebrew cognates are matched by regular sound correspondence plus a shared gloss word in Strong's definition; check them before relying on them.

leads.title: talqafu: a swallow word concentrated in Moses
leads.summary: تَلْقَفُ (talqafu, “swallow”) occurs in 3 verses; 3 of them (100%) are in the Moses narrative, which is 7% of the Quran, across 3 surahs. The more common same-gloss word خَسَفَ (khasafa, 8 verses) has only 0% of its verses there.
evidence: p = 3.4e-04 (hypergeometric, verse level), q = 1.1e-03.

leads.title: Who are the Quran's Sabians?
leads.summary: The Quran names the Sabians (al-Ṣābiʾūn) beside Jews and Christians. Candidates include the Mandaeans, the pagans of Harran, and Elchasaite baptists.
evidence: A proposed etymology links the name to Aramaic/Mandaic ṣbaʿ 'immerse', which would fit a baptist group.

leads.title: Sargon and Moses: the infant in the sealed basket
leads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian Sargon Birth Legend has a baby placed in a reed basket sealed with bitumen, set on the river, and raised by a water-drawer. Exodus 2 and the Quran's Moses (into al-yamm) share the motif.

passages.note: papyrus basket daubed with bitumen and pitch
cast into the tābūt and the yamm

evidence: Shares the yamm passages with lead yamm-sea.
The bitumen sealing is a specific shared detail between Sargon and Exodus.

leads.title: Whoever saves one life
leads.summary: Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 teaches that destroying one life is like destroying a world, and saving one is like saving a world. Quran 5:32 states the same principle as decreed for the Children of Israel.
evidence: The Quran explicitly frames it as a precept for the Children of Israel.
Mishnah manuscripts differ: some read 'a single life', others 'a single life of Israel'. Compare which reading the Quran matches.

leads.title: Dara Shikoh's Upanishads reach Schopenhauer
leads.summary: Dara Shikoh translated 50 Upanishads into Persian as the Sirr-i Akbar (1657). Anquetil-Duperron's Latin version (Oupnek'hat, 1801–02) is how Schopenhauer read them.

passages.ref: Dara Shikoh, Sirr-i Akbar (1657); Majmaʿ al-Baḥrayn (1655)

evidence: Majmaʿ al-Baḥrayn ('the meeting of the two seas') takes its title from Quran 18:60.

leads.title: Seven Sleepers and the People of the Cave
leads.summary: Youths fleeing persecution sleep in a cave for centuries and wake to a changed world. Told in Syriac (Jacob of Serugh), Greek, and Latin sources, and in Quran 18:9–26.

passages.ref: Jacob of Serugh, homily on the Sleepers of Ephesus
Gregory of Tours, Passio septem dormientium

evidence: The Quran's debate over how many sleepers there were (18:22) suggests the audience knew competing versions.

leads.title: tannūr: the oven that boiled at the Flood
leads.summary: Akkadian tinūru (oven) reached Aramaic, Hebrew, and Arabic. In the Quran's Noah narrative the sign of the Flood is that the tannūr boiled over.
evidence: The loan chain is established. The motif link (a hot or boiling flood) is the lead to investigate.

leads.title: Plotinus as the 'Theology of Aristotle'
leads.summary: An Arabic paraphrase of Plotinus' Enneads IV–VI circulated as the 'Theology of Aristotle' (al-Kindi's circle, 9th c.) and shaped Islamic Neoplatonism.

leads.title: Ancient treaty form and Deuteronomy's covenant
leads.summary: Deuteronomy follows the structure of ancient Near Eastern vassal treaties: preamble, history, stipulations, deposit, witnesses, curses and blessings.
evidence: Mendenhall (1954) argued for the Hittite model. Many scholars now consider Neo-Assyrian treaties the closer parallel. Which source is closer is the open question.

leads.title: al-yamm: the sea word reserved for Moses
leads.summary: The Quran's usual word for sea is bahr, but al-yamm appears 8 times across 4 surahs, always in the Moses/Pharaoh narrative. It is the Semitic sea word shared with Hebrew yam, Ugaritic Yam, and Mandaic yama, and borrowed into New Kingdom Egyptian.

lexical.gloss: Sea, the sea god opposed to Baal

passages.text: فَٱنتَقَمْنَا مِنْهُمْ فَأَغْرَقْنَـٰهُمْ فِى ٱلْيَمِّ بِأَنَّهُمْ كَذَّبُوا۟ بِـَٔايَـٰتِنَا وَكَانُوا۟ عَنْهَا غَـٰفِلِينَ
passages.note: Pharaoh's people drowned in the yamm

passages.text: أَنِ ٱقْذِفِيهِ فِى ٱلتَّابُوتِ فَٱقْذِفِيهِ فِى ٱلْيَمِّ فَلْيُلْقِهِ ٱلْيَمُّ بِٱلسَّاحِلِ يَأْخُذْهُ عَدُوٌّ لِّى وَعَدُوٌّ لَّهُۥ
passages.note: Infant Moses cast into the yamm (two occurrences)

passages.text: فَأَتْبَعَهُمْ فِرْعَوْنُ بِجُنُودِهِۦ فَغَشِيَهُم مِّنَ ٱلْيَمِّ مَا غَشِيَهُمْ
لَّنُحَرِّقَنَّهُۥ ثُمَّ لَنَنسِفَنَّهُۥ فِى ٱلْيَمِّ نَسْفًا
passages.note: The golden calf scattered into the yamm

passages.text: فَإِذَا خِفْتِ عَلَيْهِ فَأَلْقِيهِ فِى ٱلْيَمِّ وَلَا تَخَافِى وَلَا تَحْزَنِىٓ
passages.note: Moses' mother told to cast him into the yamm
Pharaoh and his army cast into the yamm

passages.text: فَأَخَذْنَـٰهُ وَجُنُودَهُۥ فَنَبَذْنَـٰهُمْ فِى ٱلْيَمِّ وَهُوَ مُلِيمٌ
passages.note: Pharaoh and his army cast into the yamm
Pharaoh's officers drowned in yam suf

evidence: 8 occurrences of the lemma, verified with the Quran word concordance (root ي م م); the other root hits are the unrelated verb tayammum (2:267, 4:43, 5:6).
Dispersion: 4 surahs (7, 20, 28, 51), 1 narrative. Concentrated in one story while spread across the text.
Synonym-choice skew: bahr is the general word for sea elsewhere in the Quran.
Egyptian ym is a Semitic loanword, so this is shared Semitic vocabulary fitting the Egyptian setting, not an Egyptian borrowing into Arabic.
